message.content:
During the nineteenth‑century art world, **Auguste Rodin’s “Le Penseur” (“The Thinker”)** emerged as arguably the single most celebrated sculpture. Created between 1877–1881, it captured widespread attention because:

| Feature | Why It Matters |
|---------|----------------|
| **Iconic pose** – A seated male figure hunched over his head, embodying deep contemplation | Became a universal symbol of intellectual effort; reproduced worldwide |
| **Technical mastery** – Rough textures juxtaposed with smooth surfaces illustrate Rodin’s innovative approach | Demonstrated new possibilities beyond classical idealism |
| **Public reception** – Initially exhibited at Paris Salon, later acquired by Musée Rodin & sold into private collections globally | Its popularity spread through exhibitions, prints, and eventually mass reproductions |

Other contemporaneous masterpieces—such as *Gates of Hell* (1895) and *The Burghers of Calais* (1909)—were also influential, yet none matched the enduring cultural penetration of *Le Penseur*. Thus, when historians refer to the most famed sculpture of the era, they almost always point to Rodin’s work.
